sections.h2: Selling a house in Grand Forks
sections.html:
The seat of Grand Forks County lies on the Red River of the North's western bank, just below the mouth of the Red Lake River. At 837 feet and about 29.3 square miles, it is 74 miles from Fargo-Moorhead and 145 miles from Winnipeg. Population went from 1,705 in 1880 to 59,166 in the 2020 census, thanks to early railroads and to the University of North Dakota, which opened in 1883. An Air Force base added thousands of jobs starting in 1954.

Education, defense and health care drive the economy here, so owners who rented to students, faculty or service members often sell after a tenant moves out, on a schedule they did not pick.

sections.h2: The 1997 flood and what it left behind
sections.html:
The April 1997 Red River flood devastated the city. It led to a new levee system and a greenway where homes once stood.

1997 flood measureFigure
Crest at East Grand Forks, April 2254.35 feet (flood stage 28 feet, 1979 record 48.8 feet)
Damage near Grand Forks and East Grand Forks$3.6 billion
Downtown buildings destroyed by fire, April 1911, including 60 apartments
Dike system cost, reported a decade later$400 million

Levees went up over the following decade, and many residents had to move. Where their homes stood is now the Greater Grand Forks Greenway. For a house close to the river, your insurer and the city can tell you its flood zone.

Before listing, look at the basement and the sump pump. A house that took on water in a recent spring should come with invoices and photos for the buyer.

Summers are warm and the climate is humid continental, yet freezing temperatures have been recorded in every month. Precipitation averages about 21.7 inches a year and snowfall about 48.4 inches, with extremes of minus 43 degrees Fahrenheit and 109. Because of that range, buyers study the roof, furnace and insulation.

A useful habit before listing: walk the house in the coldest part of the year, or picture it that way. Note where drafts come in, how the furnace sounds, and whether the attic is dry. Fixing a small problem, or at least disclosing it, usually costs less than a price cut after a buyer finds it.

Every rental unit needs a Certificate of Occupancy here, rent charged or not, and since 2006 one- and two-family rentals have also needed a license. Each rental is inspected roughly every five years, with earlier visits after complaints.

What inspectors check:

  • Heat that holds every occupied room at 68 degrees, measured three feet above the floor
  • Two or more off-street parking spaces, scaled to bedroom count
  • Smoke detectors, egress, wiring and railings, judged by the code in force when the building went up
  • A cap of four unrelated people per unit
  • No junk or junk vehicles on the property when the certificate issues

An owner who ignores the rules can be cited in municipal court, and a judge may order the unit vacated. Selling a rental? Check the certificate first, because the buyer will want to see it.

sections.h2: The County Recorder's role in a sale
sections.html:
Deeds and other documents that affect title go on file permanently at the Grand Forks County Recorder's Office, 151 South 4th Street, phone 701-780-8262.

You will not pay a deed or mortgage tax, because North Dakota has none. Plain copies are $1.00 a page, and certified copies are $5.00 for the first page and $2.00 for each page after that. For recording fees, ask the office or your title company.

State disclosure law requires a seller of a home with up to four units to put material facts in writing. Century Code 47-10-02.1 exempts sales by a mortgagor in default, foreclosure sales and transfers by estate fiduciaries.

Statewide, a full real estate tax payment by February 15 earns 5 percent off, and the alternative is a pair of installments due March 1 and October 15. The Grand Forks County Treasurer can confirm what your parcel owes. The title company pays that from your proceeds when the sale closes, and a payoff dated for closing day avoids surprises.

sections.h2: Selling when you are behind on payments
sections.html:
You can sell at any point before a foreclosure sale, and the state's process leaves room to act. Lenders go through court, usually after 30 to 90 days' notice, and a borrower has 30 days from the notice to reinstate the loan.

Once a sale happens, redemption generally runs 60 days. No deficiency judgment is allowed on owner-occupied residential property of four or fewer units on up to 40 contiguous acres. Military families near the base also get added protection from the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act. An attorney can explain your options.

A cash offer is a quick route, since it buys the house as it stands. We promise no price before seeing it. Weigh it against listing, counting repairs, commissions and time.

sections.h2: What to line up before closing
sections.html:
Your take-home from a Grand Forks sale depends on three figures: what you owe the lender, what you owe the county in tax, and what the Recorder charges to file. Order each early, and ask for numbers that hold through closing day. For a rental, add the Certificate of Occupancy to the stack.

  • A payoff letter from your lender
  • A tax balance from the Grand Forks County Treasurer
  • The Certificate of Occupancy and any inspection history, if tenants live there
  • Flood insurance papers and flood zone details for a house near the river
  • Your deed, or estate papers if the house was inherited

Once these are in one folder, a buyer or title company can estimate your net within a day or two. That works the same way for a listing or a cash sale, and it spares you surprises at the closing table.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works here
sections.html:
Cash buyers purchase the house in its present state. Repairs, staging and open houses are off the table, and no lender appraisal comes between the offer and closing. That suits a house that needs work, a unit a tenant just left, or a deadline set by a military move or new job.

A title company still handles the paperwork. It checks title, gathers the tax and mortgage payoffs and pays them from your proceeds, and then the Recorder's Office files the deed. If the house has flood history, rental problems or deferred maintenance, a cash buyer prices those in from the start, so you do not negotiate repair requests after an inspection.

Compare any offer with the cost of listing: repairs, commissions and the months of carrying costs while you wait for a buyer's loan.

faqs.q: Is Grand Forks still at risk of flooding?
faqs.a: A new levee system was completed about ten years after 1997, and the old floodplain became the Greenway. Ask the city and your insurer about your parcel.

faqs.q: Does Grand Forks require rental licensing?
faqs.a: One- and two-family rentals have been subject to a licensing requirement since 2006, and every rental needs a Certificate of Occupancy.

faqs.q: Is there a deed tax when I sell a Grand Forks house?
faqs.a: No. North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax. Recording and title fees are separate.

faqs.q: What happens if I miss mortgage payments in Grand Forks?
faqs.a: The lender usually sends a notice 30 to 90 days before filing suit, and you have 30 days to pay the past-due amount. A judge must approve a foreclosure sale.

faqs.q: When are Grand Forks County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Real estate tax can be paid in full by February 15 for a 5 percent discount, or in installments due March 1 and October 15. Call the Treasurer for your balance.
